Chapter 1 – How Dynasties Stay in Business
Section 1: The Roots of Permanent Power

Dynasties do not rise and fall in the United States — they entrench. The Rockefellers, Waltons, Kochs, and Pritzkers are not just names on business pages; they are the architects of a system where wealth is preserved indefinitely while the people around them lose homes, jobs, pensions, and lives. Their power isn’t about brilliance or innovation. It’s about designing machinery that outlives individual lifespans: foundations, trusts, and family offices that guarantee the family name keeps feeding on the public long after the founder is dead.

The Rockefeller fortune began with oil. The Waltons built theirs on poverty wages at Walmart. The Kochs leveraged pipelines and chemicals. The Pritzkers built empires in Hyatt hotels, Chicago real estate, and healthcare. The details differ, but the tools are the same: create permanent vehicles to shield assets from taxation, pump billions into think tanks and universities to rewrite laws, and cycle political donations until elected officials are obedient. These families never truly die — their money ensures their control continues.

The Tools They Built

Foundations were sold to the public as charity, but they are warehouses of wealth. The law requires a payout of just 5% each year, and families treat that minimum as a maximum. The “donations” are carefully targeted: a university economics department to argue against labor unions, a medical school to endorse “cost control” that really means denial of care, or a think tank to write the next tax loophole. The assets compound untouched while the receipts of their “generosity” show up as PR wins.

Dynasty trusts take it further. In South Dakota, Nevada, and Delaware, families park fortunes in trusts designed to last centuries. Inheritance tax becomes meaningless; the money never returns to the public. A Koch fortune or a Pritzker fund can now pass through dozens of generations untouched, immune to redistribution. Family offices manage this all in-house — trillions under management, larger than the hedge fund industry, yet barely regulated. These structures guarantee that the same family names appear in Forbes lists from the 1920s through the 2020s, uninterrupted.

Wages vs. Costs: The Engine of Extraction

The proof of their preservation is in the suffering of everyone else. In the 1940s, the median household income was around $1,200 per year, and rents in Massachusetts could be as low as $30 a month. A single income was enough to support a family. By the 1980s, the picture had changed: union power broken, wages stagnated, while dynastic fortunes exploded. The 2000s brought globalization, outsourcing, and debt expansion. Wages barely moved, but costs soared.

By the 2020s, Massachusetts families faced median rents of $1,200–$3,000 per month. Median household income was about $96,000, but for working-class families in Springfield, Holyoke, or Worcester, nearly half of that income vanished into housing and healthcare bills before food or heat were even covered. Evictions rose sharply, with families forced into shelters or scattered across towns, children losing schools and stability. Pregnant women evicted during pregnancy gave birth earlier and to smaller babies. The cycle of harm is written into bodies, not just balance sheets.

The dynasties thrive because the system they wrote ensures wages stay flat while costs spiral upward. Every dollar squeezed out of a paycheck becomes a dividend in their trust.

War as Business

Wars are not tragedies to these families; they are business opportunities. Rockefeller oil fueled the engines of two world wars and reaped windfall profits from every Middle Eastern conflict. Raytheon, born in Massachusetts and later folded into RTX, profited from WWII, the Cold War, Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan, and now Ukraine. Lockheed, Boeing, Northrop — the names change on the weapons, but the contracts and the board memberships stay the same.

Every war means billions in taxpayer dollars redirected to contractors. Every missile launched, every drone strike, every armored vehicle destroyed is another line of profit. The Kochs bankroll think tanks that push for intervention, while their pipelines profit from the chaos that follows. When energy prices spike in war, Exxon, Chevron, and Koch industries record record profits. Ordinary families pay higher heating bills; dynasties collect.

If wars keep repeating with the same winners and the same losers, then war is not failure — it is policy.

The Human Toll

The consequences are not abstract. In Springfield, Massachusetts, pension funds were gambled away under the watch of boards captured by asset managers like State Street and BlackRock. Thousands of retirees saw promised benefits eroded while executives collected fees no matter what. In Boston, rents doubled and tripled while REITs and dynastic real estate trusts securitized rent streams and sold them on Wall Street. Families were displaced, communities hollowed out. In Holyoke and Worcester, opioid deaths surged, fueled by Sackler family profiteering, while public health budgets were slashed to pay for tax breaks that enriched developers and asset managers.

Nationally, Black homeownership sits at around 44%, compared to 74% for whites — a gap unchanged since the 1960s. Home equity is the foundation of middle-class wealth, and without it, Black families remain trapped in cycles of debt. Hospitals deny care based on algorithmic cost formulas while CEOs pocket bonuses. Children are born smaller, sicker, and poorer while dynastic fortunes compound untouched.

Closing Logic

The story is simple and brutal: the same names, the same tools, the same results. Foundations and trusts hoard wealth. Political donations buy laws. Wars produce contracts. Wages stagnate. Costs explode. Families lose homes. Children die younger. And the dynasties never lose.

If the same families have ruled for a century, and if conditions for ordinary people only worsen, then logic demands the conclusion: dynasties stay in business by keeping everyone else in suffering.

Historically, the burden on students has worsened dramatically.

1970s: Average annual tuition at a public university was about $500; at a private university, about $2,000.

2020s: Public tuition averages $10,000+, private tuition exceeds $40,000–50,000. Costs have increased more than 200% in real terms since the 1980s. Median household income did not keep pace.

As of 2025, the median U.S. household income is about $80,600. One year at Harvard consumes nearly the entire income of a median family.

The human toll is severe: students delay marriage, children, homeownership. Credit scores are crushed by default. Entire generations are trapped in repayment. Minority and first-generation students are hit hardest. Black graduates, on average, owe $25,000 more than white graduates four years after graduation. For-profit colleges, many funded by Wall Street private equity, leave students with worthless degrees and mountains of debt.

Universities present themselves as non-profit institutions, but their behavior is indistinguishable from corporations:

They raise tuition even when endowments grow.

They expand administrative payrolls while cutting tenure-track faculty.

They invest in industries that harm students’ futures.

They suppress labor organizing among graduate students and adjuncts.

Ricky’s experience — programs that promised education and help but delivered barriers and debt — is the same model at scale. Universities lock doors for the poor while selling seats to the wealthy. They tell you education is the path out of poverty, but then they chain you to debt that ensures you never escape.

The numbers prove it:

$1.7 trillion in student debt outstanding.

43 million borrowers carrying balances.

10% of borrowers in default or serious delinquency.

Harvard endowment: $50 billion.

UMass Boston students: nearly half food/housing insecure.

IF universities have more money than ever before,
AND students have more debt and less security than ever before,
THEN higher education is not failing. It is succeeding at its true purpose: preserving elite wealth while extracting maximum dollars from the next generation.

The toll is generational: families bankrupted, dreams deferred, graduates turned into indentured workers for decades. Universities stay in business because debt keeps students and families captive long after the last exam is taken.

Chapter 4 – How Banks Stay in Business
Section 1: The Architecture of Debt and Control

Banks sell themselves as the backbone of the economy — “trusted partners” that help families save, buy homes, and build businesses. In truth, their model has always been the same: extract from depositors, leverage risk, privatize profits, socialize losses. Ricky’s story — blocked from fair treatment, denied by courts, doors slammed shut on education and business — mirrors exactly what banks have done to entire communities for decades: refuse credit to those who need it, extend predatory loans to those who can be trapped, and always find a way to make the public pay when bets go bad.

From Savings to Speculation

In the 1940s, banks functioned under strict rules. The Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 kept commercial banks (savings, loans, mortgages) separate from investment banks (speculation, securities). Depositors were protected, and risk-taking was capped. Median household income was ~$1,200 per year, and ordinary families could deposit savings and expect stability. The top 1% controlled ~11% of wealth — still a concentration, but far less than today.

By the 1980s–1990s, deregulation dismantled Glass-Steagall. Banks merged, creating conglomerates that controlled both deposits and investment arms. Citibank merged into Citigroup. Bank of America swallowed local banks nationwide. JPMorgan Chase consolidated into a global behemoth. Each merger expanded systemic risk.

At the same time, banks weaponized credit. Redlining practices — literally drawing maps to deny mortgages to Black neighborhoods — guaranteed segregation and suppressed Black wealth for generations. Predatory lending pushed subprime mortgages on vulnerable families in the 1990s and 2000s. Credit cards became profit engines: by 2000, Americans carried $650 billion in credit card debt. Today, it’s $1.3 trillion. Interest rates, late fees, and penalties became a permanent tax on working-class families.

The 2008 Financial Collapse

The crash revealed the model in its purest form. Banks packaged toxic mortgages into securities (MBS, CDOs), sold them globally, and bet against their own customers through credit default swaps. When it collapsed, households lost $19 trillion in wealth. Black and Latino families lost half their net worth. But banks were bailed out with $700 billion (TARP) plus trillions in Federal Reserve liquidity.

JPMorgan Chase: $25 billion in bailout funds.

Bank of America: $45 billion.

Citigroup: $45 billion.

Goldman Sachs: $10 billion.

Morgan Stanley: $10 billion.

None of the executives went to prison. Bonuses returned within a year. Families were left in foreclosure court while bankers reaped record pay. Ricky’s court experience — evidence discounted, outcomes predetermined — was the exact model: the system protects institutions, not people.

Banks Today: Bigger Than Ever

Since the crash, the “too big to fail” banks are bigger.

JPMorgan Chase: assets over $4 trillion (2025).

Bank of America: ~$3.2 trillion.

Citigroup: ~$2.4 trillion.

Wells Fargo: ~$1.9 trillion.

Together, the top four U.S. banks control ~50% of all banking assets.

They continue to profit from crises:

COVID-19 pandemic: banks processed billions in PPP loans, skimming fees while small businesses closed. Many loans went to large chains and well-connected firms.

Student debt: banks and loan servicers securitized government-backed loans, creating profit streams from interest even as students defaulted.

Housing: private equity firms backed by bank credit (Blackstone, Invitation Homes) bought tens of thousands of foreclosed homes and turned them into rental empires.

The Human Toll

Wages: Real median household income in 2023 was ~$80,600 — only modest growth from ~$50,000 in 2000, while housing and education costs more than doubled.

Rent: In Boston, a one-bedroom now averages ~$3,500/month. At 30% of income, that requires ~$141,000/year household income. Median families can’t keep up.

Homeownership: peaked near 69% in the mid-2000s, now ~65%. For Black families: ~44%.

Credit access: Banks deny affordable credit to small borrowers, but flood capital to hedge funds and corporations. Starting a business without collateral is nearly impossible. In 2021, only ~9% of new business applications became employer firms.

Banks profit whether people thrive or collapse. They profit on overdraft fees when you’re broke, interest when you borrow, foreclosures when you fail, and taxpayer bailouts when their bets implode.

Why This Matters

The same institutions that refused Ricky’s fair shot are the ones that refused whole communities. The denials weren’t personal — they were systemic. Courts sided with banks in foreclosure cases just as they sided against him. Evidence didn’t matter. What mattered was protecting the institution.

IF banks grow larger after every crash,
AND their profits rise even as ordinary families lose homes,
THEN the system isn’t broken. It’s working exactly as intended: to keep banks in business by extracting from the people they claim to serve.

The toll: foreclosures, evictions, bankruptcies, businesses never started, students buried in debt. Each crisis becomes another profit cycle. Like dynasties, like the Church, like universities, banks stay in business by ensuring that you don’t.

Chapter 5 – How Insurance Companies Stay in Business
Section 1: The Business of Denial

Insurance companies promise protection — coverage for illness, accidents, disability, or death. In practice, their business model is denial. They take in premiums, invest the float, and pay out as little as possible. Ricky’s lived experience — getting sick and hospitals refusing to help, MassHealth approvals delayed or denied, courtrooms siding with insurers over patients — is the same model that has defined the industry for decades. Insurance does not stay in business by paying claims. It stays in business by not paying claims.

The Structure of the Industry

The U.S. insurance system is fragmented by design: employer-based coverage, Medicare, Medicaid, and private markets all intertwine. This fragmentation creates endless opportunities for denial. The major players have consolidated into giants:

UnitedHealth Group: revenues over $370 billion (2023), covering ~50 million members. Its Optum subsidiary controls clinics, pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and data services.

Elevance Health (formerly Anthem): revenues over $170 billion, one of the largest Blue Cross/Blue Shield operators.

CVS Health/Aetna: revenues over $350 billion, combining insurance, PBM (Caremark), and retail pharmacy.

Centene Corporation: revenues over $140 billion, specializing in Medicaid managed-care contracts.

Cigna: revenues over $180 billion, including Express Scripts PBM.

These companies are not just insurers — they are vertically integrated empires. They control doctors, pharmacies, data, and insurance simultaneously. They decide which drugs are covered, which procedures are “medically necessary,” and which claims are “experimental.”

The Denial Machine

Denial comes in many forms:

Utilization management: insurers require prior authorization for procedures, often delaying care until it is too late.

Medical necessity criteria: insurers deny based on opaque rules that prioritize cost over need.

Coding games: hospitals code cases as “bad debt” or “charity care,” while insurers classify them as uncovered.

Out-of-network traps: patients treated in emergencies discover bills denied because the provider was not “in network.”

In Massachusetts, MassHealth (Medicaid) contracts with insurers like Boston Medical Center HealthNet Plan, Tufts Health Public Plans, and national players like Centene. Each contract is worth billions. Every denial that saves the insurer money is profit. Ricky’s experience — getting sick and not receiving help — is the human version of a line item on an insurer’s balance sheet.

Historical Context: Wages vs. Premiums

1970s: Employer coverage was the norm. Premiums consumed ~6% of household income.

1990s: Premiums rose faster than wages. Average annual family premium: ~$5,000.

2020s: Average annual family premium exceeds $23,000. Wages have not kept up. Median household income (~$80,600 in 2023) cannot absorb these costs without debt.

Medical bankruptcies exploded. A 2019 study found 66.5% of bankruptcies in the U.S. were tied to medical issues. Even insured patients are ruined by deductibles, co-pays, and uncovered charges.

Medicaid & Medicare: Privatized Profits

Insurers stay in business by tapping government programs. Medicaid managed-care contracts hand billions in taxpayer money to companies like Centene, Molina, and UnitedHealth. These contracts are supposed to deliver care for the poor, disabled, and elderly. In practice, they are cash cows. Centene alone has settled multiple cases for defrauding Medicaid — including a $1.25 billion multi-state settlement (2022) over inflated pharmacy claims.

Medicare Advantage, run by private insurers, is another profit engine. Companies overbill by upcoding patient risk scores. A 2020 report estimated $16 billion in overpayments annually. UnitedHealth and Humana are among the biggest beneficiaries.

COVID-19: A Case Study

During the pandemic, insurers reported record profits. Claims for elective procedures fell while premiums continued to flow. UnitedHealth’s 2020 profits exceeded $15 billion, even as patients struggled to access care. Hospitals overflowed, but insurers profited by paying out less.

The Human Toll

For ordinary people:

Premiums consume a growing share of income.

Denials delay or prevent treatment, leading to deaths that could have been avoided.

Medical debt is the leading cause of bankruptcy.

Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries are treated as revenue streams, not patients.

For Ricky, denial wasn’t abstract — it was lived reality. Needing help and being told no, waiting on approvals that never came, filing appeals that disappeared into bureaucratic silence. What happened to him has happened to millions.

Why This Matters

Insurance companies present themselves as safety nets, but the evidence shows otherwise. They exist to protect shareholders and executives:

UnitedHealth CEO Andrew Witty: compensation over $20 million (2022).

CVS CEO Karen Lynch: compensation over $21 million.

Meanwhile, patients die waiting for authorizations. Families are bankrupted. Courts side with insurers, just as they sided against Ricky, dismissing evidence of harm.

IF insurers profit more by denying care than delivering it,
AND courts, regulators, and politicians allow it,
THEN the insurance industry does not protect health. It monetizes sickness and stays in business by making sure patients lose.

The toll: preventable deaths, bankruptcies, suicides, children losing parents too soon. Denial is not a mistake. It is the product.

Chapter 6 – How Hospitals Stay in Business
Section 1: Care as a Revenue Stream

Hospitals are framed as places of healing, where lives are saved regardless of circumstance. The truth is harsher: hospitals are financial institutions first, patient-care centers second. They stay in business not by curing, but by billing. Ricky’s lived experience — walking into hospitals sick and being ignored, shuffled into denial codes, or handed bills instead of treatment — is the lived experience of millions. Hospitals do not stay solvent by delivering care. They stay solvent by extracting revenue from sickness, debt, and government programs.

The Business Model of Modern Hospitals

Hospitals in the United States generate over $1.4 trillion in annual revenue. Most operate under “non-profit” status, which exempts them from paying taxes. But “non-profit” is branding: the largest systems function like corporations, with CEOs earning millions and aggressive billing departments suing patients.

Massachusetts examples:

Mass General Brigham (formerly Partners HealthCare): annual revenue exceeds $18 billion. CEO Anne Klibanski was paid $5.3 million in 2021. Even while collecting billions in state and federal funds, the system sued patients for unpaid bills.

Baystate Health: controls hospitals across Western Massachusetts, reporting ~$3 billion in annual revenue. At the same time, it sued patients in Springfield District Court, often over bills of just a few hundred dollars.

Boston Children’s Hospital: revenues over $2.8 billion. Its endowment, alongside Harvard’s, is invested in Wall Street portfolios.

Hospitals like these report “community benefit” spending to justify tax exemptions. But “benefit” often means accounting tricks: charity care reported on paper while billing departments send patients to collections.

Coding Care Into Profits

The financial engine of hospitals is coding:

DRGs (Diagnosis-Related Groups): Medicare pays hospitals fixed amounts based on diagnosis codes, incentivizing upcoding to higher-paying categories.

ICD-10 denial codes: insurers reject claims based on technicalities, while hospitals classify unpaid bills as “bad debt” or “charity.”

Charge masters: hospitals publish inflated sticker prices for procedures (e.g., $40,000 for a knee replacement), then “negotiate” discounts with insurers. Patients without coverage are hit with the full charge.

In practice: a patient like Ricky walks in sick. The hospital decides whether treatment is reimbursable. If not, the visit becomes uncompensated care — and the patient is left with bills, collections, and ruined credit.

Consolidation and Monopoly Power

Hospitals have consolidated into mega-systems:

CommonSpirit Health: $34 billion in revenue.

Ascension Health: $28 billion.

Trinity Health: $21 billion.

HCA Healthcare (for-profit): $60 billion.

These systems dominate regional markets, eliminating competition. In Massachusetts, Mass General Brigham controls a massive share of care in Boston and beyond, dictating prices across the state. Consolidation gives hospitals leverage in negotiations with insurers, but patients are collateral.

Government Subsidies and Exploitation

Hospitals collect billions in government subsidies:

Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements: the lifeblood of hospital finances.

340B drug pricing program: hospitals buy drugs at steep discounts, then bill insurers at full price. The margin becomes pure profit.

COVID-19 relief: hospitals received tens of billions in pandemic aid, even as many furloughed staff and continued suing patients.

Despite subsidies, hospitals close in poor and rural areas because they are “unprofitable.” In Massachusetts, multiple community hospitals shuttered over the last two decades, forcing patients to travel farther while mega-systems grew richer.

Historical Context: From Community Care to Corporate Empires

1940s–1960s: Hospitals were community anchors, many run by local churches or municipalities. Care was often subsidized, and executives earned modest salaries.

1980s: DRGs introduced, turning care into billing categories. Non-profit hospitals began to behave like corporations.

2000s: Mergers accelerated, CEOs began earning millions.

2020s: Hospital systems function as hedge funds with operating rooms, controlling real estate, investments, and lobbying networks.

The Human Toll

Patients: Denied care, sued for bills, saddled with medical debt (leading cause of U.S. bankruptcies).

Workers: Nurses and frontline staff underpaid, overworked, and silenced when they speak out. During COVID, hospitals collected billions in aid while nurses reused masks and risked their lives.

Communities: Rural closures leave millions without access to emergency care. Urban consolidation raises costs for everyone.

Ricky’s reality — sick but ignored, filed away as a denial code — is the distilled truth of the system: hospitals protect their ledgers first.

Why This Matters

Hospitals claim the mantle of healing, but their practices show otherwise. They lobby against universal care, expand billing departments, and hire lawyers to pursue patients.

In 2019, Johns Hopkins Hospital was exposed for suing hundreds of low-income patients in Baltimore.

In Massachusetts, Baystate and Mass General Brigham pursued collections while reporting “charity care.”

Nationwide, “non-profit” hospitals avoid tens of billions in taxes annually by claiming community benefits they often fail to deliver.

IF hospitals grow richer while patients grow sicker and poorer,
AND denials and lawsuits rise as executives cash bonuses,
THEN hospitals do not stay in business by healing. They stay in business by monetizing sickness and externalizing suffering.

The toll: patients bankrupted, lives shortened, families destroyed by bills, children losing parents too soon. Care is incidental. Revenue is the mission.

Chapter 7 – How Pharmaceutical Companies Stay in Business
Section 1: Profit Before Patients

Pharmaceutical companies market themselves as engines of innovation — bringing miracle drugs and vaccines to save lives. But their real business model is not discovery, it is monopoly. They stay in business by controlling patents, hiking prices, and lobbying governments to protect their profits. Ricky’s experience of getting sick, hospitals refusing to help, and insurers playing games with “covered” versus “not covered” is inseparable from pharma’s playbook: if a drug is priced out of reach or kept off formularies, treatment never happens. Lives are collateral, revenue is the priority.

Patents: The Golden Locks

Drug companies depend on patents that grant 20 years of monopoly pricing. When a patent nears expiration, they engage in “evergreening” — making minor changes (new delivery system, combination pill) to extend exclusivity. Generic competition is delayed, often through legal intimidation.

Humira (AbbVie): America’s best-selling drug for arthritis and autoimmune conditions. Since approval in 2002, AbbVie built a fortress of over 100 patents. In the U.S., it blocked generics until 2023. By then, Humira had generated $200 billion in global sales.

Insulin: discovered in 1921 and sold for $1. Yet in the 2000s–2010s, three companies (Eli Lilly, Sanofi, Novo Nordisk) dominated 90% of the market and raised prices from ~$20 per vial in the 1990s to $300+ per vial by the 2010s. Patients rationed insulin; some died.

Patents aren’t about recouping R&D — they are about ensuring monopolies.

R&D Myth vs. Reality

Drug companies claim high prices are necessary to fund research. In reality, much research is taxpayer-funded. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) invests over $45 billion annually in medical research. Nearly every blockbuster drug in recent decades originated with NIH or university labs. Pharma companies acquire rights later, privatizing publicly funded science.

Example: The COVID-19 vaccines. Moderna’s mRNA platform was heavily funded by NIH and DARPA. The U.S. government poured $10 billion into vaccine R&D and procurement under Operation Warp Speed. Moderna’s 2021 revenues: $18.5 billion. Pfizer-BioNTech’s: $37 billion. Executives pocketed millions in bonuses and stock sales. Taxpayers paid twice: once to fund, again to buy back at monopoly prices.

Pricing Games

Pharma prices are untethered from reality:

Cancer drugs regularly cost $100,000+ per year.

Hepatitis C drug Sovaldi (Gilead) launched at $84,000 per course. Gilead recouped its entire R&D investment in less than a year, then kept cashing in.

Orphan drugs for rare diseases often exceed $500,000 annually.

The U.S. allows direct-to-consumer advertising, unlike most countries, fueling demand for branded drugs while generics are sidelined. PBMs (pharmacy benefit managers) — often owned by insurers like CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, OptumRx — negotiate rebates with manufacturers, but keep margins opaque. Patients see only higher co-pays and deductibles.

Lobbying: Buying Protection

The pharmaceutical lobby is the most powerful in Washington. In 2022 alone, drug companies spent over $375 million on lobbying, more than any other industry. Top firms — Pfizer, AbbVie, Johnson & Johnson, Amgen, Eli Lilly — fund armies of lobbyists to block price regulation. For decades, Medicare was legally prohibited from negotiating drug prices, thanks to pharma lobbying. That changed only recently, but implementation will be slow and limited.

Executives are lavishly compensated:

Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla: $33 million (2022).

Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel: $398 million in stock sales (2021–2022).

AbbVie CEO Richard Gonzalez: $26 million (2022).

Meanwhile, patients ration insulin, skip cancer treatments, or go bankrupt from hepatitis C cures.

Historical Context

1940s–1960s: Drug discovery was steady, often collaborative with universities and public labs. Prices were modest. Penicillin was cheap, widely available.

1980s: Bayh-Dole Act allowed universities and small companies to patent publicly funded research, accelerating privatization of science.

1990s–2000s: Blockbuster drugs (Lipitor, Prozac, Nexium) generated tens of billions. Marketing eclipsed R&D spending.

2010s–2020s: Specialty drugs, biologics, and gene therapies priced in the hundreds of thousands. Pharma became more about acquisitions and patents than discovery.

The Human Toll

Patients: Denied lifesaving drugs because of cost. Thousands die annually from insulin rationing in the U.S. alone.

Families: Medical bankruptcies tied to drug costs.

Global inequality: ARVs for HIV/AIDS were kept at $10,000/year in the 1990s until activists forced generic production in Africa. Millions died while patents were defended.

Public trust: Shattered by scandals — Vioxx (Merck, 60,000 deaths), OxyContin (Purdue/Sackler, fueling the opioid epidemic with 500,000+ U.S. overdose deaths).

Ricky’s personal story — hospitals refusing help, systems choosing codes over care — is the same story here: access denied because revenue comes first.

Why This Matters

Pharma companies stay in business by monopolizing cures, hiking prices, and lobbying for protection. They profit whether patients live or die. Public money funds their science, but private profits are protected at all costs.

IF patients die because drugs are priced out of reach,
AND pharma executives and shareholders enrich themselves from monopolies,
THEN the pharmaceutical industry is not about healing. It is about extraction, and it stays in business by turning illness into a permanent revenue stream.

The toll: preventable deaths, generations locked in debt, public science privatized for private gain. The cure exists — but you can’t have it unless you can pay.

Chapter 8 – How Defense Contractors Stay in Business
Section 1: War as a Recurring Revenue Stream

Defense contractors present themselves as “patriotic” guardians of national security. Their ads show soldiers reunited with families, fighter jets soaring with flags. But their true model is not patriotism, it is profit. They stay in business by ensuring that wars never end, budgets only grow, and taxpayers keep footing the bill. Ricky’s experience in court — evidence ignored, outcomes predetermined — mirrors how defense contractors operate: the outcome of every war is already decided. The public loses, but the contractors win.

The Business Model

War is a subscription service. Every bomb, bullet, missile, and jet produces steady revenue. Defense contractors don’t need victory; they need contracts. That’s why conflicts drag on for decades. The incentives are clear:

Raytheon/RTX (based in Massachusetts): annual revenues $68 billion (2022), deriving billions from missile systems like the Patriot and Javelin. Contracts spike whenever conflict erupts — Iraq, Afghanistan, Ukraine.

Lockheed Martin: the world’s largest defense contractor, revenues $67 billion, driven by the F-35 fighter jet program — the most expensive weapons system in history at $1.7 trillion lifecycle cost.

Northrop Grumman: $36 billion in revenue, specializing in drones, bombers, and nuclear modernization.

General Dynamics: $39 billion, including tanks, submarines, and IT contracts.

Boeing Defense: $26 billion, manufacturing aircraft, satellites, and weapons.

These companies operate with guaranteed profits: “cost-plus” contracts reimburse all expenses, then add a percentage for profit. The risk is zero. The incentive to overrun costs is built into the model.

Iraq and Afghanistan: Case Study in Recurring Revenue

The wars after 9/11 created a 20-year feeding frenzy.

Total cost to taxpayers: $8 trillion (Brown University’s Costs of War Project).

Halliburton/KBR (once led by Dick Cheney) received $138 billion in contracts.

Raytheon, Lockheed, Boeing, Northrop, General Dynamics split tens of billions in weapons sales.

Private security firms (Blackwater, later Academi) were paid billions, with little oversight.

The wars killed over 900,000 people (combatants and civilians) and displaced 38 million. But for contractors, the outcome was a balance sheet: quarterly revenues, stock buybacks, dividends.

Since 2022, U.S. aid to Ukraine has exceeded $113 billion, much of it for weapons.

Raytheon/RTX: surged on missile sales.

Lockheed Martin: Javelin and HIMARS demand skyrocketed.

General Dynamics: artillery and tanks replenished.

Executives call conflicts “growth opportunities.” In 2022, Raytheon CEO Greg Hayes told investors, “We are seeing some benefit… everything that’s being shipped into Ukraine, that’s all going to have to be replenished.” War equals orders; orders equal profit.

Political Capture

Defense contractors lock in influence with lobbying and donations. In 2022, the industry spent over $120 million on lobbying. They fund both Republicans and Democrats. Former generals and Pentagon officials cycle directly into boardrooms. This revolving door guarantees that budgets grow.

The Pentagon’s budget for 2024: $886 billion — larger than the next 10 countries combined. The “defense” budget is not about defense. It is a public-to-private pipeline.

Massachusetts: The Home Front

Raytheon/RTX is a Massachusetts anchor. Its headquarters in Waltham (now Arlington, VA officially, but major operations remain in MA) ties the state’s economy to war. Thousands of engineers and machinists rely on contracts. State pensions (PRIM, PERAC) invest in defense stocks. The state profits when wars expand. The cycle Ricky saw in pensions and contracts — money diverted away from citizens — plays out here: your retirement is tied to someone else’s missile.

Historical Context

1940s–1950s: WWII and Cold War build the “military-industrial complex” Eisenhower warned about in 1961.

Vietnam: 20 years of contracts; Raytheon and others profited while 58,000 Americans and millions of Vietnamese died.

1980s: Reagan military buildup doubled defense budgets, enriching Lockheed and Northrop.

2000s: Iraq/Afghanistan wars became privatized bonanzas for contractors.

2020s: War on terror morphs into Cold War 2.0 — China, Russia, Ukraine — ensuring endless justification for trillion-dollar budgets.

The Human Toll

For citizens:

Trillions diverted from healthcare, education, housing.

Soldiers killed or maimed. Veterans denied care by the VA.

Civilians abroad slaughtered. Entire nations destabilized.

At home, infrastructure collapses while bombs roll off assembly lines.

For Ricky, the echo is clear: systems that ignored abuse, courts that ignored evidence — the same logic: protect the institution, protect the contract, protect the profit.

Why This Matters

Defense contractors don’t need victory, they need continuity. Every escalation is profit. Every budget line is revenue.

IF wars generate guaranteed profits regardless of outcome,
AND contractors fund the politicians who approve budgets,
THEN war is not a failure. It is a business model.

The toll: millions dead, trillions wasted, a planet destabilized — but dividends secure.

Chapter 9 – How Landlords & Real Estate Trusts Stay in Business
Section 1: Turning Homes Into Securities

Housing should be the simplest human need: a roof, four walls, stability for families. But in the United States, housing is not treated as shelter. It is treated as an asset class — a financial product to be sliced, securitized, and squeezed. Landlords and real estate trusts (REITs) don’t stay in business by providing homes; they stay in business by extracting maximum rent and flipping properties into investment vehicles. Ricky’s story — rising rents, unstable housing, courts that side with landlords — is the lived story of millions.

The Shift: From Shelter to Asset

In the 1940s–1960s, housing was relatively affordable. A single income could often support a mortgage. Postwar programs like the GI Bill expanded homeownership — though redlining excluded Black families from the benefits.

By the 1980s–1990s, financialization changed everything. Mortgages became bundled into securities. Wall Street created mortgage-backed securities (MBS), feeding global investors. Housing shifted from a place to live into a product to be traded.

By the 2000s, the bubble burst. Subprime mortgages were sold to millions of families. When it collapsed in 2008, 10 million households lost their homes. But the system didn’t end. It evolved. Wall Street firms that helped cause the crash — Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan — bought up foreclosed homes in bulk. They turned them into rental empires.

Corporate Landlords

Invitation Homes (founded by Blackstone): owns over 80,000 single-family rental homes across the U.S. Tenants report rent hikes, neglected maintenance, aggressive evictions.

Equity Residential (Sam Zell’s REIT): owns tens of thousands of apartments, including in Boston and Cambridge.

AvalonBay Communities: owns 80,000+ units nationwide, including luxury towers in Massachusetts.

Vornado Realty Trust: controls billions in commercial and residential properties.

These corporations operate as REITs — Real Estate Investment Trusts. REITs receive special tax treatment: they avoid corporate income tax if they pay out 90% of income as dividends. Wall Street loves them. Pension funds, including Massachusetts PRIM and PERAC, invest heavily in REITs. That means workers’ retirements are tied to the same landlords raising their rents.

Massachusetts: The Housing Crisis Made Policy

Boston rents (2025): average ~$3,500 for a one-bedroom. To afford this without being cost-burdened (30% of income), a household must earn ~$141,000 per year. Median household income in Massachusetts: ~$96,000. The math doesn’t work.

Homeownership: peaked at 69% nationally in the mid-2000s, now ~65%. For Black families: ~44%. In Boston, the Black homeownership rate is ~34%, compared to ~69% for whites. This gap has barely moved since the 1960s.

Evictions: In Springfield, Worcester, Boston, and Holyoke, eviction filings surged post-COVID. Landlords exploit “summary process” courts that fast-track cases, often without tenants having legal representation. Ricky’s fear of courts siding with landlords reflects reality: the system is engineered to process tenants out.

How the Model Works

Acquire Properties: During crises (2008 crash, COVID), corporations buy homes cheap.

Raise Rents: With market consolidation, they hike rents faster than wages.

Neglect Repairs: Cutting costs maximizes cash flow.

Evict Quickly: Courts fast-track evictions, tenants lack representation.

Financialize Rent: Rental income streams are securitized into bonds, sold to investors.

The home you live in is someone else’s dividend.

Historical Numbers

1940s: Median rent $30/month ($600 today). Median income ~$1,200/year. Rent was ~30% of income.

1980s: Median income ~$20,000. Average rent ~$300/month. Still manageable.

2000s: Median income ~$50,000. Average rent ~$800–$1,000.

2020s: Median income ~$80,600. Average rent in Boston ~$3,500. Rent now consumes 40–50% of median income.

Wages barely quadrupled since the 1940s. Rents increased tenfold. The canyon widened, swallowing renters whole.

The Human Toll

Families spend half their income on rent, leaving little for food, healthcare, or education.

Evictions destabilize children, forcing school changes and trauma.

Communities fracture as gentrification drives displacement.

Black and Latino families denied mortgages for decades remain renters, while white wealth compounds through home equity.

For Ricky, housing instability and courts siding with landlords aren’t personal accidents. They’re the business model.

Why This Matters

Landlords and REITs do not stay in business by providing affordable shelter. They stay in business by maximizing extraction.

IF wages stagnate while rents rise,
AND corporate landlords and REITs profit from every eviction and hike,
THEN housing is not a right. It is a financial product, and tenants are revenue streams.

The toll: evictions, homelessness, intergenerational poverty, entire cities hollowed out by speculation. The home became a commodity, and the landlord became a Wall Street firm.

Chapter 10 – How Media Companies Stay in Business
Section 1: Controlling the Story, Monetizing Attention

Media companies present themselves as guardians of democracy — informing the public, holding power accountable, giving citizens the facts. In reality, their survival depends on advertising revenue, political access, and narrative control. They stay in business not by telling the truth, but by deciding which truths are profitable to tell. Ricky’s experience — courts that ignored evidence, officials who redacted abuse reports, hospitals that buried denials in codes — is mirrored here. The media filters out the ugliest parts of the system, sanitizing crimes into “isolated incidents” and turning systemic abuse into “personal misfortune.”

The Architecture of Media Power

The U.S. media is controlled by a handful of conglomerates:

Comcast (NBCUniversal): $121 billion in revenue (2023). Owns NBC News, MSNBC, CNBC, Universal Pictures, Sky.

Disney: $88 billion. Owns ABC News, ESPN, Marvel, Hulu.

Paramount Global: $30 billion. Owns CBS, Showtime, MTV, Comedy Central.

Warner Bros. Discovery: $43 billion. Owns CNN, HBO, Warner Bros., Discovery Channel.

Fox Corporation: $14 billion. Owns Fox News, Fox Sports, Fox Broadcasting.

News Corp: $10 billion. Owns The Wall Street Journal, New York Post.

Together, these six corporations control the vast majority of what Americans watch, read, and hear. Add Big Tech — Google (Alphabet, $307 billion), Meta (Facebook/Instagram, $135 billion), Amazon ($574 billion), Apple ($383 billion), TikTok/ByteDance ($120 billion) — and you have a consolidated oligopoly.

How They Monetize

Advertising: Media companies sell you — your attention, your behavior — to advertisers. News is a vehicle for ad revenue. Stories that threaten advertisers (Big Pharma, banks, defense contractors) are softened or spiked.

Access Journalism: Politicians and CEOs grant interviews to outlets that play nice. Reporters who push too hard are sidelined.

Entertainment Over Substance: “If it bleeds, it leads.” Sensational stories draw viewers. Complex financial corruption — like PRIM funneling pensions to BlackRock — gets buried under celebrity gossip.

Narrative Framing: Corporations and donors fund “think tanks” that supply ready-made op-eds and talking points. Media repeats them uncritically.

Massachusetts: Local Press Hollowed Out

Boston Globe: once a robust investigative paper, now owned by John Henry (Red Sox billionaire). It has broken important stories (clergy abuse), but operates within the constraints of owner and advertiser interests.

Springfield Republican / MassLive: gutted by layoffs. Local corruption (Baystate lawsuits, DA Gulluni’s donors) receives minimal coverage.

Worcester Telegram & Gazette: owned by Gannett, the largest newspaper chain. Gannett cuts newsrooms to funnel profits to shareholders.

The result: communities lose watchdogs. Courts, hospitals, landlords, insurers operate with impunity because no one reports the patterns. Ricky’s cases — ignored, tampered, dismissed — barely surface in public discourse.

Historical Context: The Shrinking Window

1940s–1960s: Newspapers thrived on circulation and ads. Investigative journalism exposed McCarthyism, Watergate. The top 1% wealth share fell; watchdog media paralleled broader accountability.

1980s–1990s: Deregulation allowed consolidation. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 let companies own multiple stations and newspapers in one market. Media giants merged. Local voices died.

2000s: The internet gutted ad revenue. Craigslist and Google Ads siphoned billions. Newsrooms downsized. “Churnalism” — press releases repackaged as news — replaced investigations.

2010s–2020s: Social media platforms became gatekeepers. Algorithms reward outrage, not truth. Conspiracies thrive, but systemic financial corruption is ignored.

Who Pays the Piper?

Pharma Ads: The U.S. is one of two countries allowing direct-to-consumer drug advertising. Billions flow into networks like CNN, Fox, MSNBC. Stories about drug pricing? Muted.

Defense Contractors: Lockheed, Boeing, Raytheon sponsor “special coverage” of wars on cable news. Anchors feature generals on payroll as “analysts.”

Finance: Bloomberg, CNBC rely on Wall Street access. Harsh criticism of banks is rare.

Executives profit handsomely:

Comcast CEO Brian Roberts: $32 million (2022).

Disney CEO Bob Iger: $27 million.

Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch: $22 million.

Meanwhile, journalists are laid off in droves.

The Human Toll

Citizens receive curated narratives instead of full truths.

Local corruption (pension raids, abuse cover-ups, healthcare denials) goes unreported.

Whistleblowers are silenced or ignored.

Communities are fed outrage cycles while elites consolidate wealth.

For Ricky, this meant his abuse reports, evidence of tampering, and denials never gained traction in the press. If the media doesn’t report it, it “didn’t happen.” This selective blindness keeps the machine running.

Why This Matters

Media companies do not stay in business by telling the truth. They stay in business by protecting advertisers, courting power, and feeding distraction.

IF media revenue depends on the very corporations harming the public,
AND journalists who push too far are silenced,
THEN media is not a watchdog. It is a gatekeeper.

The toll: citizens uninformed, abusers unpunished, corruption unchallenged, democracy hollowed out. Without truth, no reform is possible.

Chapter 11 – How Technology Companies Stay in Business
Section 1: Data as the New Oil, People as the Product

Technology companies present themselves as innovators — connecting people, making life easier, democratizing information. But their real business model is surveillance, control, and monopoly. They don’t stay in business by serving people. They stay in business by owning people’s data, manipulating their behavior, and crushing competitors. Ricky’s experience — systems that ignored abuse, courts that ignored evidence, hospitals that ignored his health — is echoed here: tech platforms know everything, but they decide what matters, what is hidden, and who profits.

The Titans of Control

The so-called “FAANG” companies (Facebook/Meta, Apple, Amazon, Netflix, Google/Alphabet) — joined by Microsoft and TikTok/ByteDance — dominate modern life:

Alphabet (Google/YouTube): revenue $307 billion (2023), >80% from advertising.

Apple: $383 billion, profiting from hardware monopolies and app store fees.

Microsoft: $244 billion, from software subscriptions and cloud dominance.

Amazon: $574 billion, half from retail, half from AWS cloud contracts.

Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp): $135 billion, nearly all from ads.

TikTok (ByteDance): $120 billion, rising fast.

Together, these companies represent over $10 trillion in market capitalization. They’re bigger than most national economies.

The Real Product: You

Tech companies market products (phones, apps, cloud), but their core asset is data. Every search, click, like, purchase, GPS ping, and voice command is harvested. Google tracks your searches, Gmail, YouTube. Meta tracks your social network, photos, messages. Amazon tracks purchases, Alexa conversations. Apple claims privacy, but monetizes app ecosystem fees. Data is sold to advertisers and, often, shared with governments.

This is not “free.” You are the product. As the saying goes: if you’re not paying for it, you’re not the customer — you’re the commodity.

Monopolies in Disguise

These companies crush competition:

Google pays Apple $20 billion annually to be the default search engine on Safari. This excludes competitors.

Amazon undercuts sellers on its platform, then launches its own copycat products.

Facebook/Meta bought Instagram and WhatsApp to prevent rivals.

Microsoft bundled software to destroy Netscape and others, later buying LinkedIn, GitHub, and now Activision.

Antitrust enforcement has been weak. In the 1940s–1970s, antitrust broke up Standard Oil, AT&T, and constrained monopolies. Since the 1980s, deregulation allowed tech giants to consolidate into today’s oligopoly.

Government Contracts

Tech companies profit not only from consumers but from governments:

Amazon Web Services (AWS): dominates cloud computing, holding CIA and Pentagon contracts worth billions.

Microsoft Azure: won the $10 billion JEDI contract (later split) to run defense cloud.

Palantir: founded with CIA seed funding, builds surveillance software used by ICE and police.

Google: collaborates with governments despite employee protests (Project Maven AI drone contracts).

These contracts entwine Big Tech with military and intelligence power, blurring lines between public surveillance and private profit.

Historical Context: From Tools to Control

1940s–1970s: Tech was hardware — radios, TVs, mainframes. Profitable, but constrained.

1980s–1990s: Personal computers and the internet democratized tools — but Microsoft, AOL, and Yahoo already began consolidating.

2000s: Google, Facebook, Amazon rise by harvesting data. iPhone (2007) makes smartphones surveillance machines.

2010s–2020s: Consolidation peaks. Five companies control most online activity. AI becomes the next frontier, but built on the same exploitative data models.

Wages, Wealth, and Work

Tech promised high-paying jobs and innovation. In reality:

Gig economy: Uber, Lyft, DoorDash classified workers as “independent contractors,” denying benefits. Millions hustle for survival, while executives profit.

Automation: Jobs replaced by algorithms, while productivity gains flow only to shareholders.

Wealth: Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg — fortunes exceeding $100 billion each. Meanwhile, the median U.S. worker’s wages barely outpace inflation.

In the 1940s, top wealth concentration was ~11%. Today, the top 1% hold ~40%. Much of that is locked in tech stock valuations.

The Human Toll

Privacy eroded: every message, search, and purchase recorded.

Addiction engineered: algorithms maximize engagement, fueling anxiety, depression, polarization.

Workers exploited: warehouse injuries at Amazon, gig workers unpaid, content moderators traumatized by reviewing graphic content.

Communities silenced: stories like Ricky’s buried by algorithms that prioritize profit-driven content.

Why This Matters

Tech companies don’t stay in business by serving humanity. They stay in business by owning the infrastructure of modern life and charging rent on it.

IF data is harvested and sold without consent,
AND monopolies suppress competition while profiting from surveillance,
THEN technology is not liberation. It is enclosure — and we are the product.

The toll: broken trust, stolen privacy, manipulated elections, monopolized knowledge, fortunes built on digital extraction. Innovation becomes exploitation, and tech stays in business by ensuring dependency.

Chapter 12 – How Energy Companies Stay in Business
Section 1: Profiting from Scarcity and Crisis

Energy companies frame themselves as “powering progress” — keeping the lights on, fueling cars, heating homes. The reality: they stay in business by manufacturing scarcity, manipulating markets, and externalizing costs onto the public. Ricky’s lived experience — bills spiking, utilities refusing accountability, courts siding with corporations — mirrors the larger energy playbook: extract maximum profit while shifting risk and harm onto everyone else.

The Giants of Energy

ExxonMobil: revenue $344 billion (2023). Profits: $56 billion in 2022, the highest in its history.

Chevron: revenue $246 billion (2023). Profits: $36.5 billion (2022).

BP: revenue $241 billion. Profits: $27.7 billion (2022).

Shell: revenue $381 billion. Profits: $40 billion (2022).

ConocoPhillips: revenue $78 billion. Profits: $18.7 billion (2022).

Utilities and regional monopolies:

Eversource (MA, CT, NH): revenue $12 billion (2023). Profits: $1.4 billion.

National Grid (UK/US): revenue $34 billion (2023). Profits: $4 billion.

These companies dominate essential resources: oil, gas, electricity. Consumers cannot opt out. Energy is not a choice; it is survival.

The Business Model: Manufacture Scarcity

Energy profits depend on scarcity and volatility. When supply tightens or crises hit, prices surge. Companies then post record profits:

1970s oil shocks: OPEC embargoes quadrupled prices. Exxon, Chevron, and others reaped billions.

2000s Iraq War: oil hit $147/barrel in 2008. Energy giants soared while households paid $4+ per gallon.

2020s Ukraine War: natural gas and oil prices spiked. Exxon posted $56 billion profit in 2022 — while households in New England saw winter heating bills double.

Utilities mirror this model. In Massachusetts, Eversource and National Grid secured rate hikes even as executives took multimillion-dollar salaries. Customers were told to conserve while utilities funneled dividends to shareholders.

Subsidies and Political Capture

Despite record profits, energy companies feast on subsidies:

U.S. fossil fuel subsidies total $20 billion annually (tax breaks, drilling incentives).

Globally, subsidies top $7 trillion (IMF, 2022) when accounting for hidden costs (pollution, climate).

Utilities benefit from guaranteed rate structures approved by state regulators. These boards are often staffed by former industry executives.

Lobbying is massive. Exxon, Chevron, BP, and Shell spend tens of millions annually to block climate policy. Utilities fund local politicians to guarantee rate approvals.

Externalized Costs

The industry dumps costs onto the public:

Climate change: storms, fires, floods caused by fossil fuel emissions cost trillions globally.

Health impacts: air pollution kills ~200,000 Americans annually. Asthma, cancers, heart disease — costs borne by taxpayers and families.

Cleanup: oil spills (Exxon Valdez, BP Deepwater Horizon) cause billions in damage. Settlements rarely cover true costs.

Companies knew. Internal Exxon documents from the 1970s showed climate scientists warning executives about CO₂ and warming. Publicly, Exxon denied. Privately, it prepared rigs for rising seas. Profits came first.

Historical Context

1940s–1960s: Energy cheap, consumption expands. Oil majors grow rich but stable.

1970s: Oil crises prove volatility = profit.

1980s–1990s: Deregulation and globalization expand markets. Climate denial campaigns launched.

2000s: Wars in Middle East fuel prices. Renewable energy lags as fossil giants dominate.

2010s–2020s: Climate disasters multiply. Companies greenwash (Exxon pledges “net zero by 2050”) while expanding oil and gas projects.

Massachusetts: Local Impact

Eversource and National Grid raised rates repeatedly. In 2022–2023, households saw winter bills double. Meanwhile, Eversource’s CEO Joe Nolan collected $7.4 million in compensation.

Offshore wind projects are slow-walked, while utilities secure guaranteed profits regardless of generation mix.

Low-income households face shutoffs. Ricky’s experience with bills that couldn’t be paid, utilities unresponsive, and regulators siding with corporations is exactly the model.

The Human Toll

Families forced to choose between heat and food.

Elderly and sick die during cold snaps or heat waves.

Neighborhoods poisoned by refineries, gas leaks, and toxic dumps.

Children born into asthma corridors while executives report record profits.

Globally, climate displacement pushes millions from homes. Wars over oil and gas continue to kill. Meanwhile, shareholders receive dividends and buybacks.

Why This Matters

Energy companies claim to “power progress,” but they profit from scarcity, destruction, and dependency.

IF every crisis leads to record profits for oil majors and utilities,
AND the costs of pollution, climate, and health are pushed onto the public,
THEN energy is not a neutral commodity. It is a weaponized business model.

The toll: higher bills, poisoned communities, a destabilized climate, and generations robbed of stability. Energy companies stay in business by keeping the public captive to fuel and power they control — while presenting themselves as saviors.

Chapter 13 – How Food & Agriculture Corporations Stay in Business
Section 1: Feeding People as a Commodity, Not a Right

Food should be the most basic human necessity — the thing no one goes without. But in America and globally, food is treated not as nourishment but as a commodity. Agribusiness giants, seed monopolies, meat processors, and retail chains don’t stay in business by ending hunger. They stay in business by controlling supply chains, inflating prices, and externalizing costs onto workers, farmers, and consumers. Ricky’s experience — scraping by while corporations raked profits, watching government programs fail to deliver what they promised — mirrors how food and agriculture exploit the poor while claiming to “feed the world.”

The Giants of Agribusiness

Cargill: revenue $177 billion (2022); privately held, one of the richest family companies in the world.

Archer Daniels Midland (ADM): revenue $101 billion (2022).

Bunge: revenue $67 billion (2022).

Tyson Foods: revenue $53 billion (2022); controls much of the U.S. meat supply.

JBS: the largest meat processor globally; revenue $76 billion.

Monsanto (acquired by Bayer): seed and chemical giant; Roundup, GMO crops.

Nestlé: revenue $104 billion (2022); dominates packaged food and bottled water.

Walmart: the largest grocer in America; food sales > $200 billion annually.

Together, these corporations control seeds, fertilizers, processing, and distribution.

Seeds and Chemicals: The Monopoly at the Root

Farmers cannot simply plant seeds. Most commercial seeds are patented. Monsanto (Bayer), DuPont (Corteva), and Syngenta control over 60% of the global seed market. Patents forbid seed saving. Farmers must buy new seeds annually — and herbicides to match.

Example: Monsanto’s Roundup Ready soybeans. Farmers who tried to save seeds were sued. Between 1997 and 2010, Monsanto filed 144 lawsuits against farmers, collecting millions.

Chemical dependency is locked in: seeds engineered to resist herbicides guarantee farmers buy both seed and chemical from the same company. Costs climb, while corporate profits rise.

Processing: The Meat Cartel

Four companies (Tyson, JBS, Cargill, National Beef) control over 80% of the U.S. beef market. In poultry, Tyson and Pilgrim’s Pride dominate. In pork, Smithfield (Chinese-owned WH Group) and JBS lead.

This consolidation means price fixing. In 2020, Tyson, JBS, and others were fined for colluding to raise poultry prices. Workers in processing plants, many immigrants, are paid poverty wages and exposed to dangerous conditions. During COVID-19, meatpacking plants became epicenters of outbreaks. Companies forced workers onto lines, resulting in thousands of infections and deaths. Executives faced no criminal consequences.

Retail: Walmart and the Price Trap

Walmart is the largest grocer in America, controlling about 25% of the U.S. food retail market. It uses scale to pressure suppliers, forcing them to cut costs — often by cutting wages or squeezing farmers. Small grocers collapse. Consumers have “choice,” but the supply chain is already captured.

Food Prices and Inflation

Food prices consistently outpace wages:

1970s: Families spent ~12% of income on food.

2020s: Families still spend ~12–14%, but wages stagnated while corporate profits rose. That stability hides what’s underneath: corporations shrinking package sizes (“shrinkflation”), charging more for less, and manipulating markets.

2021–2022: Food prices surged 10–15%. Cargill, ADM, and Tyson reported record profits while families visited food banks.

Government Subsidies

The Farm Bill funnels billions in subsidies — but most go to big agribusiness. Corn and soy (largely for animal feed, ethanol, or processed foods) dominate. Fresh fruits and vegetables receive minimal support. Consumers end up with shelves full of cheap corn syrup, while healthy food is expensive.

SNAP (food stamps) is essential for millions. But Walmart and other chains are the biggest beneficiaries, capturing billions in SNAP spending. The poor are both revenue streams and scapegoats. Politicians stigmatize SNAP recipients while corporate grocers bank government money.

Historical Context

1940s–1960s: Family farms dominated. Prices were stable, local grocers supplied communities.

1970s: Nixon’s USDA pushed “get big or get out.” Agribusiness expanded.

1980s: Farm crisis — foreclosures skyrocketed, small farms crushed, agribusiness consolidated.

2000s: GMOs and chemical agriculture cemented monopoly power.

2020s: Inflation, pandemic, and war (Ukraine grain crisis) fueled record corporate profits, while food insecurity hit record highs.

Massachusetts Lens

Food deserts persist in Springfield, Worcester, and Boston neighborhoods. Supermarkets exit low-income areas, replaced by dollar stores selling processed junk.

Farmers in Western MA struggle with rising land prices and debt. Many can’t compete with industrial agribusiness.

SNAP recipients face stigma, delays, and bureaucratic hurdles — while corporations quietly profit from the same program.

The Human Toll

Families choosing between rent and groceries.

Workers in meat plants injured, sickened, and discarded.

Farmers bankrupted by debt to seed and chemical giants.

Children malnourished in the richest nation on Earth.

Ricky’s experience — systems failing to deliver the basics while corporations thrived — is the same story here: hunger is not a glitch. It is a business.

Why This Matters

Food companies don’t stay in business by ending hunger. They stay in business by ensuring dependence, monopolizing supply chains, and profiting from scarcity.

IF corporations profit more when food is scarce and prices rise,
AND subsidies flow to them while families line up at food banks,
THEN hunger is not an accident. It is a revenue model.

The toll: food insecurity, diet-related disease, debt, and despair. Food is life — but to agribusiness, it’s just another balance sheet.

Chapter 14 – How Education Systems Stay in Business
Section 1: K–12 Schools and the Testing Industry

Education is sold as the great equalizer — the way out of poverty, the guarantee of opportunity. But in practice, the U.S. K–12 system is built as a funnel: underfunded public schools for the poor, gilded private schools for the rich, and a multi-billion-dollar testing industry feeding off everyone in between. Ricky’s experience — blocked from programs that promised opportunity but delivered only more barriers — is a microcosm of the model: public education isn’t designed to equalize. It’s designed to reproduce inequality, while corporations and bureaucrats profit.

The Architecture of Public Schools

Funding inequality: In most states, schools are funded largely by local property taxes. Rich districts = well-funded schools; poor districts = crumbling buildings, underpaid teachers.

Massachusetts: touted for “world-class education,” but Boston Public Schools have struggled with overcrowding, decaying facilities, and special-ed students shunted into bureaucratic limbo. Springfield and Worcester face even deeper funding gaps.

Segregation by design: Although Brown v. Board outlawed school segregation in 1954, de facto segregation thrives through housing policy and district lines. Black and Latino students are concentrated in underfunded schools.

The Testing Cartel

Standardized testing is the lever. Companies like Pearson, ETS (Educational Testing Service), and McGraw-Hill dominate a market worth tens of billions annually.

MCAS (Massachusetts Comprehensive Assessment System): originally billed as accountability. In practice, it narrows curriculum to test prep, penalizes schools with low scores, and stigmatizes students. Ricky’s frustration with educational blockades reflects what millions of kids experience: you aren’t learning, you’re performing for a metric.

SAT/ACT: gatekeepers for college. Administered by the College Board and ACT Inc., both non-profits on paper but billion-dollar enterprises in practice. College Board reported $1.1 billion in revenue (2019), mostly from tests and prep materials.

Textbook/test publishers: Pearson controls curricula in dozens of states; its digital platforms and licensing fees lock schools into contracts.

The testing system stays in business by creating “failure.” If all students passed, the system would collapse. By ensuring a percentage always fails, test makers guarantee perpetual demand for prep courses, remediation, and new test versions.

Charter Schools and Privatization

Charter schools, pushed as “choice,” siphon public money into private management. In Massachusetts, charters in Boston and Worcester receive millions in state funding that would otherwise support traditional public schools.

Management organizations often pay executives six-figure salaries while hiring non-union teachers.

Hedge funds invest in charter networks, turning education into a portfolio asset.

Historical Context

1940s–1960s: GI Bill and postwar investment expanded opportunity — but primarily for white students. Black veterans were excluded from many benefits.

1970s–1980s: Tax revolts (e.g., Prop 13 in California) slashed school funding. Standardized testing expanded.

1990s: “No Child Left Behind” under Bush tied federal funding to test scores, exploding the testing industry.

2010s: “Race to the Top” under Obama reinforced testing and charter expansion.

2020s: Pandemic exposed digital divides. Poor students without laptops or Wi-Fi fell further behind while ed-tech companies like Zoom and Google Classroom expanded market share.

The Money Trail

Pearson PLC: $4.2 billion in annual revenue (2022), much of it from standardized testing contracts.

College Board: executives earn $500k+ salaries running a “non-profit.”

Charter networks: Success Academy (NYC) reported over $60 million in annual revenue.

Private tutoring/test prep (Kaplan, Princeton Review): multi-billion-dollar industries feeding off test anxiety.

Meanwhile, U.S. teachers earn an average of $66,000/year — far less than the value they produce — and spend hundreds of dollars of their own money on supplies.

Massachusetts Lens

Boston Public Schools: placed under state review in 2022 for “chronic underperformance.” Instead of investing, the state considered privatization.

Springfield: majority-minority student body, one of the lowest-funded districts per capita. Students face food insecurity and trauma, yet are measured by the same MCAS yardstick as elite suburban schools.

Charter push: Well-funded donors push expansion, diverting funds from public classrooms into private hands.

The Human Toll

Students: crushed under testing regimes, labeled as failures at age 8 or 10.

Families: forced to navigate bureaucracy, appeals, and hearings just to get basic special-ed services.

Teachers: demoralized, burned out, leaving in droves.

Communities: schools closed, children bused across towns, neighborhoods destabilized.

Ricky’s roadblocks in education — doors promised, then slammed shut — are not anomalies. They are policy. They guarantee that poverty reproduces poverty, while testing firms and charter managers keep cashing in.

Why This Matters

Education systems do not stay in business by uplifting every child. They stay in business by maintaining stratification:

wealthy kids fed into Ivy Leagues,

working-class kids tracked into debt,

poor kids labeled as failures.

IF schools are funded unequally,
AND testing ensures a percentage always fails,
THEN education is not a ladder. It is a filter.

The toll: generations locked into cycles of poverty, communities stripped of control, children stigmatized before they’re even adults. Education, like housing, healthcare, and justice, has been turned into another industry of extraction.

Chapter 15 – How Courts & Prosecutors Stay in Business
Section 1: Justice as a Pay-to-Play System

Courts and prosecutors claim to uphold the rule of law, protect the vulnerable, and deliver justice without bias. In reality, they stay in business by filtering justice through money, politics, and selective enforcement. Ricky’s lived experience — evidence tampered with, abuse reports ignored, judges siding with institutions, prosecutors declining to act — is not the exception. It is the model. The system is not designed to protect citizens. It is designed to protect itself and the interests of the powerful.

The Architecture of Legal Power

Courts and prosecutors operate in overlapping loops:

Judges: elected or appointed, often with donor support. Corporate attorneys and prosecutors dominate the pipeline to the bench. Few defense lawyers, almost no tenant or patient advocates, ascend.

District Attorneys: campaign donors shape priorities. In Massachusetts, DA races have been heavily funded by unions (police, corrections) and by firms tied to development.

U.S. Attorneys & DOJ: politically appointed, toggling priorities with administrations. White-collar prosecutions have plunged in recent decades.

Private Law Firms: the “shadow judiciary.” Corporate law firms (Skadden, Kirkland & Ellis, WilmerHale, Ropes & Gray) rotate attorneys into judgeships, prosecutors’ offices, and back again.

Every case Ricky lost in court — where evidence was ignored, filings dismissed, or abusers protected — reflects this larger structure: outcomes are predetermined by alignment of power and money.

Revenue Streams

Courts stay in business through:

Fines and fees: Municipal courts fund themselves by levying fines. Poor defendants are milked for revenue. In Ferguson, Missouri (2015 DOJ report), fines and fees made up 23% of city revenue. Massachusetts courts also rely on probation fees, filing fees, and “user payments.”

Civil forfeiture: Police and prosecutors seize property allegedly tied to crime. In many states, proceeds go directly into DA budgets. Between 2000–2019, law enforcement seized $68.8 billion in assets nationwide. Most seizures are never contested, because the cost of fighting is higher than the value seized.

Court surcharges: Victims forced to pay for copies of transcripts, filings, and records. Redactions are billed per page. Even FOIA filings become revenue streams.

Selective Enforcement

Justice is not applied evenly.

White-collar crime: Prosecutions have collapsed. In 1995, the DOJ prosecuted ~1,000 white-collar defendants annually. By 2020, fewer than 400. Bankers responsible for the 2008 crash? Zero prison sentences.

Drug crimes: Prosecutions soared. Black and Latino defendants disproportionately targeted. Marijuana still accounts for thousands of arrests annually, even in states where it’s legal.

Police violence: Officers almost never prosecuted. In Massachusetts, DA offices routinely decline charges, citing “insufficient evidence” even when body cams or witnesses exist.

Abuse cases: Survivors disbelieved, evidence discounted — just as Ricky experienced. Courts often side with institutions (churches, hospitals, corporations) to shield liability.

Massachusetts Lens

Hampden County DA Anthony Gulluni: recipient of union donations, criticized for light white-collar enforcement. Abuse survivors report being ignored or pressured into silence.

Massachusetts judiciary: multiple judges with prior careers in corporate defense. Decisions on housing overwhelmingly favor landlords.

Court records: fees and redactions limit access. Survivors like Ricky face an uphill battle just to get evidence admitted.

Historical Context

1940s–1960s: Courts enforced segregation, blocked labor rights, upheld corporate power. Some progress (civil rights rulings), but always contested.

1970s–1980s: “Law and order” era. Mass incarceration accelerates.

1990s: “Tough on crime” policies explode prison populations. Three-strikes laws, mandatory minimums.

2000s–2010s: War on terror expands prosecutorial discretion. Courts defer heavily to government secrecy.

2020s: Mass incarceration remains. White-collar crime enforcement collapses. Courts overwhelmed with eviction filings post-COVID, siding with landlords.

## Chapter 1, Section 1: Dynasties — Staying in Business

The Rockefeller, Walton, Koch, DuPont, Mellon, and Pritzker families don’t just inherit wealth—they engineer its permanence. From 2010 to 2025, their trusts, foundations, and family offices cemented control over Massachusetts’ hospitals, insurers, real estate, and policy, extracting billions while externalizing harm to families like Ricky’s, whose abuse reports vanished and care was denied. This is no accident; it’s a century-old design.

**Money & Ownership**: Rockefeller wealth, rooted in Standard Oil, flows through trusts and the Rockefeller Foundation (~$5B AUM, 2023). Pritzkers control Hyatt and healthcare investments via family offices. Koch Industries ($125B revenue, 2022) and Waltons (Walmart, $611B revenue) hold stakes in insurers and REITs. SEC 13F filings show BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street managing their assets, with BlackRock’s $12.5T AUM (2025) as a universal shareholder.

**Law & Loopholes**: Dynasty trusts in Delaware/South Dakota shield billions from estate taxes (IRS code 26 U.S.C. § 541). The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act doubled estate tax exemptions to $11.2M per person, saving dynasties billions. Pritzkers exploit Delaware LLCs for real estate; Kochs use shell entities for lobbying (ALEC filings).

**Public Contracts & Procurement**: CTHRU reveals $1.2B in MassHealth grants to Mass General Brigham (MGB), tied to Pritzker investments (2023 990s). Koch-backed firms secured $50M in state energy contracts (COMMBUYS). Waltons’ logistics firms won $20M in MBTA contracts (2015–2024).

**Courts & Enforcement**: MGB settled a DOJ False Claims Act case (1:18-cv-10471, D. Mass., $32M, 2021) under Healey’s AG oversight, with no charges. **Pensions & Asset Managers**: Massachusetts PRIM allocates ~$90B to BlackRock/State Street (2023 reports), which hold stakes in MGB, Walmart, and Koch firms. Pensioners face cuts while managers collect fees.

**Healthcare/Insurance Touchpoints**: MGB (Pritzker-linked) and Baystate (BlackRock-backed) dominate Massachusetts healthcare, denying care via “utilization management.” Liberty Mutual (Walton stakes) donated ~$15,000 to Healey, securing $10M in tax incentives (CTHRU).

**Labor & Wages**: Walmart’s wage suppression (median $25k/year) and Koch’s anti-union lobbying (ALEC) keep Massachusetts wages flat (~$80k median, 2023). Productivity rose 80% since 1980; wages barely 10% (BLS).

**Media/Tech & Narrative Control**: Rockefeller Foundation funds media (WBUR, $1M, 2020). Kochs back think tanks (Heritage, $50M) shaping narratives. Local papers (Boston Globe) downplay dynasty influence due to ad revenue.

**Philanthropy/Education Capture**: Rockefeller Foundation gave $10M to Harvard (990s, 2022), influencing healthcare policy. Pritzkers fund UMass ($5M, 2020), securing research favorable to their firms.

**Defense/Security Ties**: Kochs and Mellons sit on Raytheon boards (DEF 14A, 2023), profiting from $886B Pentagon budgets (2024). Donations to Baker aligned with defense grants (COMMBUYS).

**Externalities/Harm**: Koch industries’ pollution cost Massachusetts $100M in health damages (EPA, 2020). Pritzker REITs’ evictions destabilized 5,000 Boston families (2023, JCHS). Workers and communities bear the costs.
